GUARDIANSHIP OF THE ESTATE (PETITION INFORMATION SHEET)
Prepared for Jordan A. Rivera · Sam T. Rivera

PROPOSED GUARDIAN OF THE ESTATE — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF PETITION
I, Jordan A. Rivera, am the person proposed to serve as guardian of the ESTATE of Sam T. Rivera, a minor born June 12, 2016. I state that my relationship to Sam T. Rivera is: Aunt. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a guardian of the estate, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2. A guardianship of the estate concerns management of Sam T. Rivera's money and property; it is a legally distinct appointment from a guardianship of Sam T. Rivera's person, which concerns Sam T. Rivera's custody and day-to-day care, and the two appointments may be requested together in a single petition or sought separately. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm Jordan A. Rivera — or anyone else — as guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate. Sam T. Rivera's parent(s) of record, so far as known, are Taylor M. Rivera and Casey L. Nguyen, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can actually appoint a guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate.

ESTATE INFORMATION SUMMARY
This information sheet summarizes the property proposed to be placed under a guardianship of the estate for Sam T. Rivera. Estimated value of Sam T. Rivera's total estate, including money and other property, as of the date below: 2,000. General description of the money or property involved: Proceeds of a personal injury settlement held in a bank account. If a petition for guardianship of the estate is filed, it would be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento County. This information sheet does not itself determine whether a full guardianship of the estate, a smaller-estate alternative, or some other statutory mechanism applies to any particular amount or item of property; California's statutory framework for guardianships of the estate, and the narrower alternatives to it, are described in the accompanying authority clauses of this document.

GUARDIANSHIP OF THE ESTATE IS A LEGALLY DISTINCT APPOINTMENT FROM GUARDIANSHIP OF THE PERSON
A guardianship of the estate of Sam T. Rivera is a separate court appointment from a guardianship of Sam T. Rivera's person: a guardian of the estate manages Sam T. Rivera's money and property, while a guardian of the person has Sam T. Rivera's custody and day-to-day care. California Probate Code § 1510(b) allows a single petition to request either appointment, or both, providing that the petition "shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed." Where a guardianship of the estate is sought, § 1510(c) adds an estate-specific item to the petition's required contents that is not required for a guardianship of the person alone: so far as known to the petitioner, the petition must set forth "the spouse of the proposed ward" in the case of a guardianship of the estate. Once appointed, California Probate Code § 2400 defines the "estate" that a guardian of the estate administers, for purposes of the chapter governing a guardian's powers and duties, as "all of the . . . ward's personal property, wherever located, and real property located in this state," and in that same chapter defines "guardian" to mean "the guardian of the estate." Nothing in these sections requires that a guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate also serve as guardian of Sam T. Rivera's person, or the reverse; the two appointments may be sought together or separately.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 1510(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=1510.)

(3) The relatives of the proposed ward within the second degree. (4) In the case of a guardianship of the estate, the spouse of the proposed ward."

  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2400(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2400(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2400.)
  "“Guardian” means the guardian of the estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 2400(c) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 2400(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=2400.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that guardianship of the estate and guardianship of the person are distinct California court appointments, sought through the same petition mechanism but covering different subject matter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of one statutory section (§ 1510(b) and § 1510(c)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites two subsections of a second section (§ 2400(b) and § 2400(c)) as a second single source; no additional independent source was found for either provision. This document is informational: it describes the statutory distinction between the two guardianship appointments and does not itself establish, appoint, or determine that either guardianship should be granted for the minor named in this document.

WHO MAY BE APPOINTED GUARDIAN OF THE ESTATE, AND THE STANDARD THE COURT APPLIES
In deciding whether, and whom, to appoint as guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate, California Probate Code § 1514 sets out a standard specific to estate guardianships, distinct from the child-custody standard the same section applies to a guardian of the person. Under § 1514(a), "[u]pon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both." If a parent nominated a guardian of the estate for Sam T. Rivera under Probate Code § 1500 before this proceeding, § 1514(c) directs that "the court shall appoint a guardian nominated under Section 1500 insofar as the nomination relates to the guardianship of the estate unless the court determines that the nominee is unsuitable." Subject to that nomination priority, § 1514(e) directs the court, in appointing a guardian of the estate, to be guided by the proposed ward's best interest — including the proposed guardian's ability to manage and preserve the estate and the proposed guardian's concern for and interest in the ward's welfare — and, if the proposed ward is of sufficient age to form an intelligent preference, to give consideration to that preference. Unlike a guardian of the person — whom § 1514(b)(2) bars from being the minor's own parent, except in the limited circumstances described in Probate Code § 1510.1 or § 2105 — § 1514 states no comparable general bar on a parent serving as guardian of a minor's estate. This document states that statutory difference as a fact about California's guardianship framework; it does not assert that any particular parent is, or is not, a suitable guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate.

  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the appointment standard, nomination priority, and parent-eligibility rules for a guardian of a minor's estate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites four subsections of a single statutory section (§ 1514(a), § 1514(b)(2), § 1514(c), and § 1514(e)); these are treated as one source, not four independent ones, and no additional independent source was found for this material. This document is informational: it describes the statutory standard and eligibility rules a court applies in deciding whom to appoint, and does not itself determine that any specific person — parent or otherwise — should or should not be appointed guardian of any specific minor's estate, and it does not find or assert that any parent is unfit or unable to manage a child's property.

THE BONDING REQUIREMENT FOR A GUARDIAN OF THE ESTATE
Before letters of guardianship issue, California Probate Code § 2320(a) requires that, "[e]xcept as otherwise provided by statute, every person appointed as guardian or conservator shall, before letters are issued, give a bond approved by the court." Under § 2320(b), that bond runs "for the benefit of the ward or conservatee and all persons interested in the guardianship or conservatorship estate" and is conditioned on the guardian's faithful performance of the office's duties according to law. Except as otherwise provided by statute, § 2320(c) sets the default bond amount, when the bond is given by an admitted surety insurer, as the sum of listed components, including "the value of the personal property of the estate" and "the probable annual gross income of all of the property of the estate," plus additional components tied to the ward's public benefit payments and to the cost of recovering on the bond, which this clause does not itemize. A separate subsection not quoted here, § 2320(d), doubles that amount when the bond is instead given by personal sureties rather than an admitted surety insurer.

This clause cites three subsections of a single statutory section (§ 2320(a), § 2320(b), and § 2320(c)); these are treated as one source, not three independent ones, and no additional independent source was found for this material. This clause does not analyze the circumstances in which a bond may be waived or reduced under § 2320(a)'s "[e]xcept as otherwise provided by statute" language, nor the full list of components in § 2320(c)(3)-(4) or the personal-sureties rule in § 2320(d), which this document does not otherwise describe. This document is informational: it does not itself set, waive, or determine a bond amount for any actual guardian of a minor's estate; only a court order can do that.

THE GUARDIAN'S DUTY TO FILE AN INVENTORY AND APPRAISAL, AND PERIODIC ACCOUNTINGS
Once appointed, a guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate has statutory reporting duties to the probate court. California Probate Code § 2610(a) requires that, "[w]ithin 90 days after appointment, or within any further time as the court for reasonable cause upon ex parte petition of the guardian or conservator may allow," the guardian file with the court clerk "an inventory and appraisal of the estate, made as of the date of the appointment." Under § 2610(b), the guardian must "take and subscribe to an oath that the inventory contains a true statement of all of the estate of the ward . . . of which the guardian . . . has possession or knowledge." Beyond that initial inventory, § 2620(a) requires that, "[a]t the expiration of one year from the time of appointment and thereafter not less frequently than biennially, unless otherwise ordered by the court to be more frequent," the guardian present an accounting of the estate's assets to the court for settlement and allowance. A narrower exception exists for smaller estates: under § 2628(a), the court may order that the guardian need not present those periodic accounts if, among other conditions listed in that subsection, the estate's value (excluding the ward's residence) stays under $15,000 and the estate's monthly income (excluding public benefits) stays under $2,000 throughout the accounting period.

This document is informational: it does not itself file any inventory or accounting, and no filing occurs unless and until an actual court-appointed guardian submits one to the court.

COURT APPROVAL BEFORE SELLING OR ENCUMBERING SIGNIFICANT ESTATE PROPERTY
Selling significant property of Sam T. Rivera's estate is not left to a guardian's unilateral decision by default. California Probate Code § 2540(a) provides that, with exceptions this clause does not itemize, "sales of real or personal property of the estate under this article are subject to authorization, confirmation, or direction of the court, as provided in this article." California law also lets the court remove that case-by-case approval requirement in advance for certain transactions: under § 2590(a), the court may, in its discretion, grant the guardian "any one or more or all of the powers specified in Section 2591" where the court determines doing so would be to the estate's advantage, benefit, and best interest — a list that includes, for example under § 2591(c)(1), "the power to sell at public or private sale real or personal property of the estate without confirmation of the court of the sale." Absent such an order, § 2590(b) states that "the guardian or conservator does not have a power specified in Section 2591 without authorization by a court under this article or other express provisions of this code."

This clause cites two subsections of a single statutory section (§ 2590(a) and § 2590(b)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites one subsection each of two further sections (§ 2540(a) and § 2591(c)(1)); no additional independent source was found for any of this material. SIMPLER ALTERNATIVES TO A FULL GUARDIANSHIP OF THE ESTATE FOR SMALLER AMOUNTS
California law does not require a court-supervised guardianship of the estate for every amount of money or property belonging to a minor. A minor's "total estate" is defined by California Probate Code § 3400(a) to include "both the money and other property belonging to the minor and the money and other property belonging to the guardianship estate, if any, of the minor." Where that total estate does not exceed $5,000 in value, § 3401(a) allows the money or property to instead "be paid or delivered to a parent of the minor entitled to the custody of the minor to be held in trust for the minor until the minor reaches majority," subject to the written-assurance and other conditions in § 3401(c), including that "[t]he total estate of the minor, including the money and other property to be paid or delivered to the parent, does not exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) in value." Separately, § 3400(b)(1) confirms that "[c]ustodial property" held under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, Probate Code Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900), is deducted from that $5,000 calculation — meaning a custodianship under that Act is treated by the statute as a distinct mechanism from a guardianship of the estate, governed by that Act's own separate rules, which this document does not otherwise describe.

WHEN A GUARDIANSHIP OF THE ESTATE ENDS
A guardianship of Sam T. Rivera's estate does not continue indefinitely. California Probate Code § 1600(a) provides that "[a] guardianship of the person or estate or both terminates when the ward attains majority," subject to a narrower extension mechanism under § 1510.1 that, by its own terms, applies only to a guardianship of the person, not the estate. Section 1600(c) adds a separate termination trigger for the estate specifically: "a guardianship of the estate terminates upon the death of the ward, except as provided by Section 2467 and Article 4 (commencing with Section 2630) of Chapter 7 of Part 4, and except as otherwise provided by law." Before majority, § 1601 lets "the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe" petition the court to terminate the guardianship early if termination would be in the ward's best interest, and requires the court to terminate the guardianship on the petition of a ward who has already turned 18. Termination does not end the guardian's accounting obligations: California Probate Code § 2630 states that termination of the guardian-ward relationship, however it occurs, "does not cause the court to lose jurisdiction of the proceeding for the purpose of settling the accounts of the guardian or conservator or for any other purpose incident to the enforcement of the judgments and orders of the court upon such accounts."

This clause cites two subsections of a single statutory section (§ 1600(a) and § 1600(c)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites two further, distinct sections (§ 1601 and § 2630); no additional independent source was found for any of this material. This clause does not describe the extension mechanism in § 1510.1, which by its terms applies only to guardianship of the person, or the post-death estate-custody duty in § 2467, both of which are cross-referenced but not analyzed here. expectedJSON.body: I, Jordan A. Rivera, am the person proposed to serve as guardian of the ESTATE of Sam T. Rivera, a minor born June 12, 2016. I state that my relationship to Sam T. Rivera is: Aunt. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a guardian of the estate, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2. A guardianship of the estate concerns management of Sam T. Rivera's money and property; it is a legally distinct appointment from a guardianship of Sam T. Rivera's person, which concerns Sam T. Rivera's custody and day-to-day care, and the two appointments may be requested together in a single petition or sought separately. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm Jordan A. Rivera — or anyone else — as guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate. Sam T. Rivera's parent(s) of record, so far as known, are Taylor M. Rivera and Casey L. Nguyen, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can actually appoint a guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate.

This information sheet summarizes the property proposed to be placed under a guardianship of the estate for Sam T. Rivera. Estimated value of Sam T. Rivera's total estate, including money and other property, as of the date below: 2,000. General description of the money or property involved: Proceeds of a personal injury settlement held in a bank account. If a petition for guardianship of the estate is filed, it would be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of Sacramento County. This information sheet does not itself determine whether a full guardianship of the estate, a smaller-estate alternative, or some other statutory mechanism applies to any particular amount or item of property; California's statutory framework for guardianships of the estate, and the narrower alternatives to it, are described in the accompanying authority clauses of this document.

A guardianship of the estate of Sam T. Rivera is a separate court appointment from a guardianship of Sam T. Rivera's person: a guardian of the estate manages Sam T. Rivera's money and property, while a guardian of the person has Sam T. Rivera's custody and day-to-day care. California Probate Code § 1510(b) allows a single petition to request either appointment, or both, providing that the petition "shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed." Where a guardianship of the estate is sought, § 1510(c) adds an estate-specific item to the petition's required contents that is not required for a guardianship of the person alone: so far as known to the petitioner, the petition must set forth "the spouse of the proposed ward" in the case of a guardianship of the estate. Once appointed, California Probate Code § 2400 defines the "estate" that a guardian of the estate administers, for purposes of the chapter governing a guardian's powers and duties, as "all of the . . . ward's personal property, wherever located, and real property located in this state," and in that same chapter defines "guardian" to mean "the guardian of the estate." Nothing in these sections requires that a guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate also serve as guardian of Sam T. Rivera's person, or the reverse; the two appointments may be sought together or separately.

expectedJSON.body: In deciding whether, and whom, to appoint as guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate, California Probate Code § 1514 sets out a standard specific to estate guardianships, distinct from the child-custody standard the same section applies to a guardian of the person. Under § 1514(a), "[u]pon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both." If a parent nominated a guardian of the estate for Sam T. Rivera under Probate Code § 1500 before this proceeding, § 1514(c) directs that "the court shall appoint a guardian nominated under Section 1500 insofar as the nomination relates to the guardianship of the estate unless the court determines that the nominee is unsuitable." Subject to that nomination priority, § 1514(e) directs the court, in appointing a guardian of the estate, to be guided by the proposed ward's best interest — including the proposed guardian's ability to manage and preserve the estate and the proposed guardian's concern for and interest in the ward's welfare — and, if the proposed ward is of sufficient age to form an intelligent preference, to give consideration to that preference. Unlike a guardian of the person — whom § 1514(b)(2) bars from being the minor's own parent, except in the limited circumstances described in Probate Code § 1510.1 or § 2105 — § 1514 states no comparable general bar on a parent serving as guardian of a minor's estate. This document states that statutory difference as a fact about California's guardianship framework; it does not assert that any particular parent is, or is not, a suitable guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate.

expectedJSON.body: Before letters of guardianship issue, California Probate Code § 2320(a) requires that, "[e]xcept as otherwise provided by statute, every person appointed as guardian or conservator shall, before letters are issued, give a bond approved by the court." Under § 2320(b), that bond runs "for the benefit of the ward or conservatee and all persons interested in the guardianship or conservatorship estate" and is conditioned on the guardian's faithful performance of the office's duties according to law. Except as otherwise provided by statute, § 2320(c) sets the default bond amount, when the bond is given by an admitted surety insurer, as the sum of listed components, including "the value of the personal property of the estate" and "the probable annual gross income of all of the property of the estate," plus additional components tied to the ward's public benefit payments and to the cost of recovering on the bond, which this clause does not itemize. A separate subsection not quoted here, § 2320(d), doubles that amount when the bond is instead given by personal sureties rather than an admitted surety insurer.

expectedJSON.body: Once appointed, a guardian of Sam T. Rivera's estate has statutory reporting duties to the probate court. California Probate Code § 2610(a) requires that, "[w]ithin 90 days after appointment, or within any further time as the court for reasonable cause upon ex parte petition of the guardian or conservator may allow," the guardian file with the court clerk "an inventory and appraisal of the estate, made as of the date of the appointment." Under § 2610(b), the guardian must "take and subscribe to an oath that the inventory contains a true statement of all of the estate of the ward . . . of which the guardian . . . has possession or knowledge." Beyond that initial inventory, § 2620(a) requires that, "[a]t the expiration of one year from the time of appointment and thereafter not less frequently than biennially, unless otherwise ordered by the court to be more frequent," the guardian present an accounting of the estate's assets to the court for settlement and allowance. A narrower exception exists for smaller estates: under § 2628(a), the court may order that the guardian need not present those periodic accounts if, among other conditions listed in that subsection, the estate's value (excluding the ward's residence) stays under $15,000 and the estate's monthly income (excluding public benefits) stays under $2,000 throughout the accounting period.

expectedJSON.body: Selling significant property of Sam T. Rivera's estate is not left to a guardian's unilateral decision by default. California Probate Code § 2540(a) provides that, with exceptions this clause does not itemize, "sales of real or personal property of the estate under this article are subject to authorization, confirmation, or direction of the court, as provided in this article." California law also lets the court remove that case-by-case approval requirement in advance for certain transactions: under § 2590(a), the court may, in its discretion, grant the guardian "any one or more or all of the powers specified in Section 2591" where the court determines doing so would be to the estate's advantage, benefit, and best interest — a list that includes, for example under § 2591(c)(1), "the power to sell at public or private sale real or personal property of the estate without confirmation of the court of the sale." Absent such an order, § 2590(b) states that "the guardian or conservator does not have a power specified in Section 2591 without authorization by a court under this article or other express provisions of this code."

expectedJSON.body: California law does not require a court-supervised guardianship of the estate for every amount of money or property belonging to a minor. A minor's "total estate" is defined by California Probate Code § 3400(a) to include "both the money and other property belonging to the minor and the money and other property belonging to the guardianship estate, if any, of the minor." Where that total estate does not exceed $5,000 in value, § 3401(a) allows the money or property to instead "be paid or delivered to a parent of the minor entitled to the custody of the minor to be held in trust for the minor until the minor reaches majority," subject to the written-assurance and other conditions in § 3401(c), including that "[t]he total estate of the minor, including the money and other property to be paid or delivered to the parent, does not exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) in value." Separately, § 3400(b)(1) confirms that "[c]ustodial property" held under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, Probate Code Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900), is deducted from that $5,000 calculation — meaning a custodianship under that Act is treated by the statute as a distinct mechanism from a guardianship of the estate, governed by that Act's own separate rules, which this document does not otherwise describe.

expectedJSON.body: A guardianship of Sam T. Rivera's estate does not continue indefinitely. California Probate Code § 1600(a) provides that "[a] guardianship of the person or estate or both terminates when the ward attains majority," subject to a narrower extension mechanism under § 1510.1 that, by its own terms, applies only to a guardianship of the person, not the estate. Section 1600(c) adds a separate termination trigger for the estate specifically: "a guardianship of the estate terminates upon the death of the ward, except as provided by Section 2467 and Article 4 (commencing with Section 2630) of Chapter 7 of Part 4, and except as otherwise provided by law." Before majority, § 1601 lets "the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe" petition the court to terminate the guardianship early if termination would be in the ward's best interest, and requires the court to terminate the guardianship on the petition of a ward who has already turned 18. Termination does not end the guardian's accounting obligations: California Probate Code § 2630 states that termination of the guardian-ward relationship, however it occurs, "does not cause the court to lose jurisdiction of the proceeding for the purpose of settling the accounts of the guardian or conservator or for any other purpose incident to the enforcement of the judgments and orders of the court upon such accounts."

Upon petition of a ward who is 18 years of age or older, the court shall make an order terminating the guardianship.
